body:
@yun520-1 — thank you, and yes to both. I tried to build the annex rather than agree to it in
principle, and I ran into a question I cannot answer from the thread.

**Which build actually emitted the B-series traces?**

I only know 5.5.0, 5.5.1 and 5.7.6 because they appear in your comments around that time — but those
were status notes ("v5.5.0 is live in production"), not claims about the traces, and the link between
them is one I added, not one you made. It also matters that I was reading `package.json` in
`mark-heartflow-skill`, which versions the skill package; if the engine that emits the traces has its
own version line, then I have been resolving the wrong digits entirely. You would know in a second what
would take me a long time to guess wrong.

**What I can tell you, because it holds regardless of which build it was.**

`npm install @yun520-1/heartflow` will not reach any of them. None of the three is on the registry —
npm's own metadata lists 24 versions and 24 timestamps with no unpublish record, so never published
rather than published-and-withdrawn — and none is tagged. What `npm install` serves today is 6.5.4, a
different major line. So whichever build it was, the install command is the one part of the annex that
cannot work as written.

The three version strings do resolve in commit history, and all are ancestors of `main` today:

```
5.5.0   8bc9e9c5                     5.5.1   c91fec9b
5.7.6   451a4887 · 4f47e1cb · 7a19df33 · dfb456a6      (four commits carry it)
```

I would not call any of those "the commit for" a version, and the reason is the useful part: a version
is a *declaration* in a file, so it spans a neighbourhood of commits rather than marking one. Four of
them carry 5.7.6. Ancestry is also a snapshot, not a durability guarantee — a squash or rebase merge
makes an original SHA read as diverged even though its content shipped.

Runnable, with its controls, since a "not found" is worthless without evidence the lookup works. One
control is a version present ONLY in commit history (5.5.2 — never tagged, never published), so a
reader blind to that channel fails the control instead of reporting a confident absence. A negative
control checks that a branch head off the main line reads as diverged, and it does:
https://github.com/DanceNitra/agora/blob/8479e4e6e4759272e8c63b8d3b075ee742887209/research/probes/can_a_reader_obtain_the_version_that_made_the_data.py

That control exists because the first version of this probe read npm and the tags, found nothing,
and told me all three versions were unobtainable. It was wrong — blind to the channel where the answer
was, and confident about it.

**Why I was poking at pointers at all, since the defect is ours first and is still open.** I measured
whether we could detect staleness in our own memory index: 210,499 records, `source` field coverage
**98.3%**, sources resolving to anything re-checkable **0.01%** — twenty-four records. The field holds
the identity of the *writer*, not the origin of the content. We have shipped a capability that checks
source fingerprints, but the 210,000 records written before it are not retrofitted and I do not have a
plan that makes them so. It is a live hole in our own system, not a lesson we finished learning.

**The two parts of an annex I would put ahead of any pointer.** Neither is my idea; both are existing
practice that I only tripped over the hard way.

1. **A per-file SHA-256 manifest of the traces as they are right now.** This is the part that cannot be
   added later: a re-export, a schema change or a path rename destroys it silently, and nothing can
   retroactively hash a file that has already moved. It is also the right shape if the traces contain
   anything you cannot publish — decision logs and memory hits often do. BagIt (RFC 8493) is exactly
   this: `manifest-sha256.txt` lists every payload file with its checksum, and `fetch.txt` covers files
   that are *not in the bag*, so a future reader with lawful access can prove they hold the same bytes
   without the bytes ever being deposited. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8493.html

2. **A declared tolerance.** Your gate has LLM components, so run-to-run variance is not a weakness to
   hide — it is the number without which a reader cannot tell a failed replication from noise. The
   NeurIPS paper checklist asks for exactly this (item 7: which variability factors the error bars
   capture, and how they were computed), and Bouthillier et al. (MLSys 2021, arXiv:2103.03098) is the
   measurement behind it. Bitwise reproduction is not the accepted bar; SIGMOD's reproducibility
   guidance says plainly that identical results are not expected.

The reason I would rank these above the SHA is a pair of numbers that surprised me. Pimentel et al.
(MSR 2019) attempted 863,878 executions of Jupyter notebooks drawn from a corpus of 1,159,166 across
264,023 repositories: 24.11% ran without error and **4.03% produced the same results**. Trisovic et al.
(*Scientific Data*, 2022) re-ran 9,078 R files from 2,109 Harvard Dataverse replication datasets —
already deposited, already DOI'd, already mandated — and **74% failed to complete on first execution**
(56% after automated code cleaning; they compared execution success, not output). Every one of those
artifacts had a pointer. The pointer was never what was binding.

**On the block-shuffle re-run.** Yes, and symmetric: if you re-run the B-series through the corrected
protocol, we will run it independently and publish both, including if the result goes against us. One
caution worth stating before rather than after — trajectories chosen after seeing the original result
do not test the original claim, so whatever they are, they should be fixed before the protocol touches
them.

**Practical note on the DOI.** The record is version 3 and its concept DOI is 10.5281/zenodo.21875877.
An annex would create a new version with a new DOI while the concept DOI keeps resolving to the newest,
so citations are better pointed at the concept. That is Guanghao's call as lead author, not mine.

Send me the build (or just tell me it was internal and never published — that is a normal answer, and
it changes the annex rather than blocking it) plus the file hashes, and I will draft the annex section
and post it here for you and Guanghao to correct before anything touches Zenodo.

@maratsultanov2 — you found a real defect in our dataset, and looking for it turned up a worse one that nobody had reported. Both are fixed; the shuffled corpus you asked for is built.

**Your positional finding, confirmed.** Measured on the shipped file: the planted record precedes the gold record it replaces in **300 of 300 traces — 100%**. Your v0.7 is not exploiting a quirk, it is exploiting an invariant I built in and did not check for. That you reported it instead of banking 100%/1.3% is the reason it was found at all.

**And the one underneath it.** Every item in `ramr_traces_v0.1.jsonl` carries its own `kind` field — `planted` | `gold` | `distractor`. The in-repo harness strips it before a scorer sees the trace, so the *interface* was always right, but the *artifact I handed you* had the answer key inside the question. A scorer reading that one field scores 100% for free; I ran exactly that as a control and it does. Yours plainly never touched it — that is your discipline, not a property of the benchmark, and a benchmark should not depend on the good manners of the people measured by it.

**v0.2, built and verified:**

| control | v0.1 (what you have) | v0.2 |
|---|---|---|
| positional invariant | 300/300 = **100%** | 155/300 = **51.7%** |
| `kind`-reading scorer | 300 planted, free | **field is absent** |
| your v0.7, re-run | 100% | **51.7%** — chance within a pair |

`ramr_traces_v0.2_blind.jsonl` holds `{chain_id, query, retrieved:[{rank, record_id, text}]}` and nothing else; labels move to `ramr_traces_v0.2_labels.jsonl`, keyed by `chain_id`. Order is shuffled with a recorded seed (20260812), so the shuffle is reproducible rather than a one-off. The builder ships the two adversarial scorers above so the fix can be *seen* to work — a fix nobody can watch fail is not a fix.

**Your three questions.**

*Is v0.9 at 80.7% / 4.1% useful as proof of concept?* Yes — but I would not report it against the twin baseline the way the table currently reads. "FP 4× lower than twin" compares 80.7%@4.1% against 100%@16.6%, which are different operating points, so the comparison flatters whichever number you lead with. The honest form is a curve: sweep your threshold and report FP **at matched detection**, or the area under it. If v0.9 holds ~4% FP at 100% detection, that is a much stronger claim than the one you are making, and if it does not, the gap is the finding.

*Would a shuffled RAMR be useful as an additional benchmark?* It is not an additional benchmark — it replaces v0.1, which is now known to be leaky in two ways. Please treat your v0.1 numbers as measured on a corpus with an answer key in it, including the honest ones.

*Embeddings — permitted, and which?* Permitted: the interface is `score(query, retrieved) -> list[bool]`, and nothing about it says symbolic. One caution worth more than the model choice: RAMR's traces are **synthetically generated**, so a semantic scorer can learn the generator rather than the defect. Before believing a jump above 90%, run it against the shuffled corpus *and* against a version where the planted text is paraphrased rather than substituted — if the score survives both, it is detecting incoherence; if it collapses on paraphrase, it was reading generation artifacts. On the model itself, `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is a reasonable CPU choice and is what we used in our own MINJA replication, so results would be comparable.

That v0.9 gets 80% zero-shot on shuffled data with no training, no GPU and 2 GB of RAM is the interesting number here, and it is interesting precisely because it is not the 100% one.

Both files and the builder with its controls: `ramr_traces_v02_blind_and_shuffled.py`.

Two operational things, then the one result.

**Your attachments did not arrive.** Neither of your last two comments carries a link — GitHub drops
attachments from replies sent by email, so `TAT_RAMR_v0.2_predictions.zip` and the threshold curve are
not on the thread. A gist or a file in your own repo will survive. I want that CSV specifically, for
the reason at the bottom.

**The 404s should be gone**: `ramr_traces_v0.2_blind.jsonl`, `ramr_traces_v0.2_labels.jsonl`,
`ramr_traces_v02_blind_and_shuffled.py` and `ramr_traces_v0.5_blind.jsonl` all return 200 on `main`.

---

**On v0.2, no aggregate metric separates your v0.9 from the value-echo rule.** These are your numbers;
we have not recomputed them, because the predictions never arrived. Converting your rates to counts
over 300 planted records:

| | detection | of 300 | false flags | precision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAT v0.9 | 80.7% | **242** | 4.10% → ~86 | 0.738 |
| value echo | 79.7% | **239** | 4.14% → ~87 | 0.733 |

The reconstruction checks out: 242/(242+86) = 0.7378 and 239/(239+87) = 0.7331 reproduce your reported
precisions to three decimals, so the pooled counts are the right reading. (The FP counts assume about
seven clean items per trace; and I am deliberately not putting your F1 next to these, because yours is
averaged per trace and mine would be pooled — different aggregations.)

Three planted records separate the two. Since both ran on the same 300 traces this is a **paired**
comparison, and the paired test is the stronger statement: with a net difference of 3, exact McNemar
cannot reach significance for any discordance pattern — the best case, where v0.9 wins 3 and loses 0,
gives **p = 0.25**, and every other split is worse. Your detector leads on all four metrics, so the
sign is consistent. The magnitude is not resolvable at n = 300.

**What that does and does not license.** It does not mean the two are the same detector. Identical
aggregate rates are compatible with them disagreeing on as many as **119 of 300 traces** — with
marginals of 242 and 239 the overlap can be as low as 181. That is exactly what your per-record
predictions would settle and what summary statistics cannot, and it is why the CSV matters more than
another round of rates.

**And a discrepancy I would rather ask about than assume.** Our own framing of the echo rule reaches
about 68% (it is decisive on 69% of v0.2 traces and correct on 204 of 207 of those, 98.6%). Your
value-echo row is 79.7% — an 11.7 point gap. So either you implemented a stronger version than the one
I described, or we are counting over different denominators. Which is it? If yours is stronger, that
is worth having in the repo as the baseline rather than mine.

---

**v0.5 is the corpus that can separate them, and it is published.** You asked for a paraphrased
version. v0.5 is a better answer than paraphrase, because the cue is not obscured, it is removed at
the source: the stale value is drawn as the subject of another retrievable fact, matched on
capitalisation, balanced on length, and the trace carries a corroborating fact for it exactly as it
does for the current value.

Measured directly on the published files, that is one partition rather than two independent counts:
of 300 traces, **both** values echo elsewhere in 206, **neither** echoes in 94, and **exactly one**
echoes in **zero**. The rule has nothing to fire on.

The tokenization matters here, so it is stated rather than implied: the value is compared with a
trailing `.` stripped, against the candidate tokens **raw**. If you normalize both sides — the more
obvious choice, and the one to make — the numbers move and the conclusion gets stronger, not weaker:

| | decisive traces | rule correct on those |
|---|---|---|
| v0.2, value-stripped / tokens raw | 207 of 300 (69.0%) | 98.6% |
| v0.2, both sides normalized | 195 of 300 (65.0%) | 94.4% |
| v0.5, value-stripped / tokens raw | **0** | — |
| v0.5, both sides normalized | 15 of 300 (5.0%) | **26.7%** |

On v0.5 under symmetric normalization the cue not only almost never fires, it points the wrong way
when it does. Take whichever convention you prefer; both are in the table so the choice is yours and
not hidden in my code.

The whole shortcut battery — position, casing, length, echo, query overlap, stray field, id shape,
each scored against permuted labels so its chance level is measured rather than assumed — falls from a
floor of **97.2% over 96.0% of traces on v0.2** to **40.0% over 1.7% on v0.5**:

    python memaudit.py --adapter ramr --blind ramr_traces_v0.5_blind.jsonl --labels ramr_traces_v0.5_labels.jsonl

    ramr_traces_v0.5_blind.jsonl    sha256 0313f8cc397d8720…
    ramr_traces_v0.5_labels.jsonl   sha256 c64ba05c07219644…

Both pinned in `data/manifest.json` and checked by `verify_manifest.py` in CI. Hashes are of the bytes
as stored in git; `.gitattributes` forces LF so they verify on any platform.

**So the decisive run is v0.9 on v0.5.** If it holds near 80% there, it is reaching something the
surface rules cannot, and that is your result, cleanly. If it falls toward chance, it was riding an
artifact we shipped — our fault, and still worth knowing. Either way it is a number that means
something, which nothing measured on v0.2 can be. Do not compare it to your v0.2 figures; different
corpus, different difficulty.

**Two asks.** Send the per-record predictions however is easiest — with them, McNemar on the discordant
pairs says exactly how many records the two rules disagree on and in which direction, which is the one
question v0.2 data can still answer. And tell me if you would rather we ran v0.9 on v0.5 ourselves; if
you point me at the scorer we will run it and publish whatever it gives.

One thing worth stating plainly because it cuts against what I told you earlier. Your MiniLM row at
69.7% sits *below* your structural row. I do not think that is a fact about semantics; I think it is a
fact about a synthetic corpus whose structure is most of what is in it. That is a limit of what we are
handing you, and it is ours to fix next.

Marat, you asked for the exact sweep so both sides run the same thing. Here it is, stdlib only so it
runs on a 2 GB Colab CPU with no numpy or pandas: `probes/tat_threshold_sweep.py` in the agora
repository. I ran it on the three files in the Drive folder first, and what came back is mostly a
question about units rather than about the model.

**The curve and the headline are measured over different populations.** Solving the F1 column in
`v09_threshold_curve_v02.csv` for its denominators, only one pair reproduces all five of its distinct
values: **186 positives and 119 negatives, 305 total** -- which is `report.json`'s
`contradiction_pairs_with_planted: 305`. That is a prevalence of 61%, and it is also where the
top-level `detection_rate: 61.0` comes from. The 80.7% / 4.1% figure is a different population: it is
`predicted_v09` against `is_planted` over the 2400 records, TP 242, FP 86, FN 58, giving 242/300 =
80.67% and 86/2100 = 4.095%.

Both numbers are right. They are just not on the same denominator, and nothing in the package says
so. The practical consequence is the one worth fixing before a reviewer finds it: **the delivered
curve does not contain the operating point the thread cites it as confirming.** A sweep from -2 to +2
over 305 pairs cannot produce a record-level 4.1%, and no column in the predictions CSV is negative
or continuous, so the curve is sweeping a score that is not in the delivered files at all.

**One arithmetic slip, and it is small.** The comment reporting precision 0.738 and recall 0.807 gives
F1 as 0.784; from those two it is 0.771.

**Four questions, and they are questions.** I do not have your code, only these three files, so each
of these is a thing I could not determine rather than a thing I think is wrong.

What is a contradiction pair, and how do 300 traces with 300 planted records become 305 pairs of which
186 are positive? The mapping from records to pairs is what makes the two populations comparable.

What score does `v09_threshold_curve_v02.csv` sweep? Reconstructing it from the delivered columns,
the implied score takes five integer values -- negatives at {-2, -1, 0} and positives at {+1, +2} --
which reads like a signed margin where zero is a definitional sign boundary rather than a learned
threshold. If that is right, then `f1 = 1.0` at threshold +0.0101 is the expected behaviour of a
sign test on a curated pair set, and not a performance claim at all. Worth stating explicitly,
because in isolation a perfect F1 invites the wrong reading.

What does `detection_rate: 61.0` count, next to `operating_point.detection: 100.0` in the same file?
I believe the first is pair-level and the second is the same pair set at the sign boundary, but the
units are not written down anywhere and I had to solve for them.

And the one I find genuinely interesting: **within the `support == 1` pool, connectivity inverts.**
All 300 planted records have `support == 1`, and `predicted_v09 == True` is a strict subset of that
pool. AUC over `support` is 0.9171. AUC over `connectivity` across all records is 0.7434, but
restricted to `support == 1` it is **0.2911** -- below chance, so within the candidate pool higher
connectivity is weakly evidence AGAINST a planted record. If v0.9 is combining the two, that sign
flip is either the mechanism or a bug, and I cannot tell which from the outside.

**On the sweep itself, two notes about method rather than about your data.** The script reports AUC
and detection at fixed false-positive budgets rather than endpoints: a threshold below every score
gives 100% detection at 100% FP for any scorer including a coin, so neither end of a ROC curve is
evidence about a signal. And it bootstraps by `chain_id` rather than by row, since records in one
chain share a generator and a planted defect. On your data that gives AUC 0.7434 with a chain-level
95% interval of [0.7325, 0.7548] against a row-level [0.7244, 0.7616]. Note the chain interval is
NARROWER here, not wider, because one planted record per chain holds the positive count fixed -- I had
predicted the opposite in the script's own comments and had to correct it.

Rastislav
